newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally, bonds fall on rate fears, dollar firmer.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally, bonds fall on rate fears, dollar firmer.

text.p: Stocks rallied for the second session in a row on Tuesday as investors snapped up technology shares, but bonds fell on renewed fears the Federal Reserve will raise rates again in July.
The dollar rose as investors flocked to safe havens amid worries about the implication of France's parliamentary election for Europe's proposed monetary union.
Coffee futures soared as continuing worries about short supplies of high-quality arabica coffee beans threatened to push the market to new 20-year highs, traders said.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 37.50 points at 7,383.41, beating Friday's record finish of 7,345.91. The market was closed Monday for the Memorial Day holiday.
The blue-chip index at one time surged to 7,394.95, just short of the 7,400 level.
But in the broader market, declining issues outnumbered advances 1,299 to 1,222 on active volume of 435 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite and the Standard & Poor's 500 indices also set second consecutive highs.

The Dow was on a roll, racing back from an early loss of nearly 40 points as it tracked the rise in International Business Machines Corp., which surged 5-1/2 to a new all-time high of 178-7/8, one day before IBM's much-anticipated two-for-one stock split.
It was the second record high in less than five trading sessions for IBM after last Wednesday's 175-1/8 -- its first record close since August 1987.
Analysts said the rally in technology stocks was rooted in positive comments on Micron Technology Inc. by an influential analyst. Micron jumped 4-3/8 to 42-5/8.
Merrill Lynch's Tom Kurlak, a longtime bull, said he expected Micron to earn even more in 1997 and 1998 than he previously expected.

"All the action was in technology today. It's contagious," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Securities. "When you like one (tech stock), you like the group, both first- and second-tier. That's the momentum that got things going."

The rally touched almost every sector of the technology group, from computer companies to chip stocks to networking firms. Even disk drive makers rebounded, recovering slightly from recent losses that were driven by fears that disk drive prices would drop further.

The stock market broke away from the downdraft in bonds, where the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 15/32, or $4.69 on a $1,000 bond, which raised its yield to 7.03 percent from Friday's close of 6.99 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The inflation-sensitive bond traders sold on news that the Conference Board's index of U.S. consumer confidence hit a 28-year high of 127.1 in May, vs. a reading of 118.5 in April.
The dollar rose to 1.7055 marks in late trading from 1.6930 marks late Friday and to 116.67 Japanese yen from 115.65 yen. Both U.S. and British currency markets were closed on Monday for holidays.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery rose 17.45 cents a pound to close at 274.30 cents, just below the 20-year high of 280 cents a pound set by the expired May coffee contract two weeks ago.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices fell sharply as talk of sufficient supply of both crude oil and unleaded gasoline put an end to the market's recent strength.

Crude oil for July delivery closed 84 cents lower at $20.79 a barrel, with June unleaded gasoline ending 1.54 cents a gallon lower at 65.38 cents and June heating oil ending 2.25 cents a gallon lower at 55.27 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index finished 19.8 points higher at 4,681.6, just 12.3 points off its all-time closing high set May 16. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average lost 153.61 points, or 0.77 percent, to finish at 19,889.89.
